national.title: Trump says US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop
national.summary: Trump backed members of his administration who are asking for $50bn to rebuild air traffic control systems in the wake of last Friday's major outage.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has said air traffic control systems that manage flights across the country are "ancient" and is pushing Congress to fund costly upgrades.

Trump called the systems "obsolete", saying they were at least "55 years old" and noted some towers were not in good shape structurally.

"It's very safe. But it's safe for a different reason because we do it very slowly," he said. "In other words, we travel slower. That's why you have lots of waits at the airport."

His remarks came a week after a historic ground stop halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the agency planned on Friday to share more information about what led to the four-hour ground stop on 13 November.

Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.

At a press briefing, Trump responded to some concerns about whether the ground stop issue was at all linked to other tech outages in the same week.

"They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."

national.title: DEA dismantles first nitazene synthesis lab in the U.S.
national.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration's forensic testing confirmed the lab in Louisiana was manufacturing etonitazene, an extremely potent synthetic opioid belonging to a class of drugs known as nitazenes.
national.body: The first nitazene synthesis laboratory in the U.S. has been dismantled by local and federal authorities. The lab, discovered earlier this month in Louisiana, was thought to be producing fentanyl. But on Wednesday, the Drug Enforcement Administration's forensic testing confirmed it was manufacturing etonitazene, an extremely potent synthetic opioid belonging to a class of drugs known as nitazenes. Nitazenes emerged in the American drug supply around 2019 and can be 80 times more potent than fentanyl. The facility, located in the basement of a residential home in Baton Rouge, was part of a drug distribution network targeted by the DEA and the East Baton Rouge Sheriff's Office. The bust was part of a three-month investigation led by local narcotics agents. Described as "large-scale" and "sophisticated," the clandestine laboratory contained approximately $250,000 in professional-grade equipment, according to the DEA.Authorities found specialized temperature-control equipment, an industrial evaporator and 58 liters of liquid in its main reactor vessel. The liquid was later confirmed to be etonitazene. This drug facility bust represents a "first-of-its-kind discovery for DEA in the United States," East Baton Rouge Sheriff Sid J. Gautreaux III said in a statement. "Every day, families across our communities are suffering the devastating consequences of illegal drugs. The emergence of substances like nitazenes makes our mission even more urgent." Louisiana has become a primary hot spot for the emerging threat of nitazenes: More than 80% of all etonitazene exhibits seized by the DEA nationwide this year have originated in the state, according to the Louisiana State Police Crime Laboratory. Earlier this year, the DEA warned it was seeing fentanyl mixed with "a dangerous array of synthetic substances," including nitazenes.60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim has spent months investigating the new, deadly synthetics in the illegal drug supply. In One Molecule at a Time, airing Sunday, Wertheim goes on a raid with the DEA. He also visits the DEA Special Testing and Research Laboratory to learn about the global pipeline of chemicals and evolving chemistry powering drug cartels' synthetic opioid production and distribution. Learn more about nitazenes and synthetic opioids in Jon Wertheim's report, Sunday on 60 Minutes.

national.summary: The Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey.
national.body: More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says.According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15.At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC. That brings the total number of reported cases to 148.Dr. Aileen Marty, an infectious disease expert at Florida International University, warned that the number of cases could rise before the ship returns to Fort Lauderdale."It's quite likely that the numbers will increase because even right now there are people incubating whatever it is," Marty said.In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan.In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated. The CDC said samples have also been collected for testing to help determine the cause of the outbreak."Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation," the CDC said on its website. "Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time."So far, the cause of the illness is unknown.Marty said several viruses or bacteria could be responsible for the symptoms, emphasizing that norovirus has not been confirmed as the cause."But tests will need to be done to determine if this is truly norovirus or another virus or a bacteria that's causing this," Marty said."Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. national.title: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
national.summary: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.
national.body:
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.

The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.

Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.

Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.

national.title: Rights groups urge sanctions after ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
national.summary: The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
national.body:
Edith M. Lederer, Associated Press Edith M. Lederer, Associated Press

UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya

The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

Myanmar's government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court's demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.

Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges.

"Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision," she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. "So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair."

While the World Court's rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

national.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
national.summary: The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
national.body:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

national.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
national.summary: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
national.body:
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."

national.title: Mayor Mamdani announces plan to shut down Rikers Island
national.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.
national.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.The city is legally required to close the troubled jail complex by August 2027. Mamdani acknowledges the city won't meet that deadline, and is now proposing a closure date of 2032, along with a sweeping overhaul of how the city handles people awaiting trial. The six-year plan requires legislative approval. The administration closed one Rikers facility earlier this year, but the rest of the complex remains open.What's in the plan"I'm proud to say New York City will close Rikers Island once and for all," Mamdani said Friday.The four new borough-based jails are designed to hold about 4,100 people. That's far fewer than the roughly 6,700 people reported in custody at Rikers in June, so the population will need to be reduced to be spread to the smaller borough jails. Rikers mostly houses people awaiting trial. Mamdani's plan calls for reducing detention and case delays. "The first jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, followed by Bronx and Queens 2031, Manhattan 2032. These jails will look and feel very different than Rikers," Mamdani said. "It is about creating a system grounded in dignity. One that recognizes the humanity of everyone who comes into contact with that system," Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards said. "In the first six months of 2025, half of the felony cases in our city took over one year to resolve. That's simply unacceptable," City Council Speaker Julie Menin said. Creating an interagency case delay task force to speed up processing, evidence sharing and expanding psychiatric bed capacity would get the inmate population down to 5,500 by 2029, according to the city's projections. Under Mamdani's plan, that's when the first replacement jail will open."We'll work across city agencies to speed up the exchange of evidence and address court backlogs. We do not want any New Yorker to spend a day longer in detention than necessary," Mamdani said. Violence and safety concerns have plagued the facility for years. Mamdani said assaults at Rikers happen at eight times the rate of similar jails, and inmates are held there nearly four times longer than the national average.His administration is putting millions toward reducing the jail population and improving conditions. national.title: Fiona's caretakers and fans mourn the beloved hippo after her death at Cincinnati Zoo
national.summary: Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many.
national.body:
CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.

Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.

The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.

Since her death, Fiona's fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats.

Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.

During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for "anyone that was going through hard times."

"The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles."

Fiona makes her debut to the media in Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo in Cincinnati, Ohio, May 2017. File photo by Liz Dufour/USA TODAY Network via Imagn Images via Reuters

national.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test
national.summary: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
national.body:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.

national.title: Court approves $7.25 billion Bayer settlement over claims Roundup weed killer caused cancer
national.summary: Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.
national.body:
David A. Lieb, Associated Press David A. Lieb, Associated Press

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.

WATCH: What science tells us about the health risks of Roundup

The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.

For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users.

Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.

Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.

In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

national.title: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
national.summary: Grieving Filipinos confront a distressing reality: their dogs and cats may not have received the send-off they paid for.
national.body:
A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

national.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
national.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
national.body:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

national.body:

Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

Victoria Milko, Associated Press Victoria Milko, Associated Press

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks in Turkey stretched into overtime Friday and delegates put off some decisions to next year, unable to find common ground on multiple issues with mutterings and protests about failure. Still, organizers remained hopeful that they could find ways the world can work together to avert the most catastrophic effects of global warming.

"We are close to the finish line but not there yet," said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, president of the two-week summit known as COP31.

During a late-night session, delegates passed a protest banner reading "failure," while a demonstrator interrupted Kurum as he spoke, shouting, "you are killing the future, you are killing the future."

"Yes, we are tired, and we have put in a great deal of effort—but we still have the capacity, right here in this hall, to convey truly meaningful messages to the world," Kurum pleaded Friday night. "By reaching a consensus, we can effect real change."

The term "fossil fuels" wasn't even mentioned in the latest draft of the final agreement — meant to address how the world will deal with climate change — sending activists and country leaders into an uproar Friday.

national.title: Trump signs Common Cents Act
national.summary: The Common Cents Act established guidelines for businesses and consumers when conducting cash transactions.
national.body: President Trump on Friday signed the Common Cents Act, which lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law. It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents. For example, if a purchase costs $10.02 after tax and a customer is short 2 cents, the tab would round down to $10 under the act. A charge of $10.04 would round up to $10.05. Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. Business advocacy groups cheered its passage. NACS, which represents the convenience and fuel retailing industry, said it creates reliable guidelines for conducting cash transactions. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended," Brennan Duckett, NACS' director of regulatory and policy, said in a statement to CBS News. "NACS members benefit directly from this law, and we are pleased to see President Trump make it official with his signature."Business owners said they faced confusion and were vulnerable to litigation before the act passed. "As a retailer, I am grateful to have established legal guidance on rounding cash transactions," Scott Zietlow, CEO and president of Kwik Trip, said in a statement Friday. "Every cash transaction that we processed in recent months was a reminder that we needed more clarity from the federal government. We've now got that clarity."

Retired Sgt. Maj. A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.

The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.

Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.

Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.

Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.

"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.

The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.

Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.

national.summary: As investigators probe what caused a New York City building collapse that killed eight people, workers and residents are painting a portrait of two trouble spots side-by-side: the apartment house that fell down and the construction site being excavated next door.
national.body:
Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press

Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — As investigators probe what caused a New York City building collapse that killed eight people, workers and residents are painting a portrait of two trouble spots side-by-side: the apartment house that fell down and the construction site being excavated next door.

WATCH: Brooklyn community leaders, residents hold meeting on building collapse

Lawsuits filed since the Nov. 11 disaster in Brooklyn cast blame in multiple directions: at the construction site owner and contractors; at an engineering firm that drew up the excavation plan; and at the owner of the building that collapsed. Several injured workers have also taken steps toward suing the city agency that polices construction safety.

A key question for investigators is whether work underway to dig a deep pit for a new building undermined the foundation of the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave., causing it to topple into the jobsite.

A lawsuit filed by five injured construction workers said the dig at 2625 Bedford Ave. lacked adequate retaining walls, shoring and underpinning to keep the adjoining building safe, and that excavation work continued even after the building's facade began to crack.

"The shoring that they were planning to keep the collapsed building up was severely insufficient," said lawyer Jonathan Damashek, who has sued on behalf of injured workers. He questioned whether the city should have approved the plans, and whether contractors' work was negligent.

national.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
national.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
national.body:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

national.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
national.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
national.body:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

national.title: Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says
national.summary: The location of the hat and the 2,400-pound animal's anatomy made removal unfeasible, the zoo said.
national.body:
The hat swallowed by beloved hippopotamus Fiona had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine, making removal "impossible", the Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio said.

Vets tried to save Fiona after she ingested the hat that ended up in her habitat by accident almost two weeks ago. But its location and the 2,400-pound (1,088 kg) animal's anatomy made removal unfeasible. She died on Thursday.

A necropsy, an autopsy performed on an animal, showed the hat was "located 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines", the zoo said on Friday.

Animal lovers were rooting for a recovery for Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017.

Cincinnati Zoo's director of animal health, Dr Mike Wenninger, said in a statement that an upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object.

"The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible," Wenninger added. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the woolen hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

national.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
national.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in the key city of Taiz, cut off from the outside world for weeks.
national.body:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

national.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
national.summary: AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
national.body:
Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption

NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

national.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
national.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
national.body:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

national.title: Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
national.summary: At the funeral for the 15-year-old who was fatally shot last month, Mamdani spoke alongside the boy's father and civil rights leaders.
national.body:
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.

Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.

"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."

"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.

His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.

Earlier this month, she told the BBC that she wanted "justice for my son", a sentiment echoed at Friday's service.

Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.

local.title: Welcoming ways to create an inclusive hospitality venue for all
local.summary: Since I began hosting WXXI’s Move to Include podcast, I’ve been thinking about where I can go to catch up with disabled sources and grab a bite to eat. But where?
local.body:
Since I began hosting WXXI’s Move to Include podcast, which delves into disability rights matters through firsthand perspectives and candid conversations, I’ve been thinking about where I can go to catch up with sources and grab a bite to eat.

And then my mind goes blank. Where are the inclusive dining spots?

Places where someone using a wheelchair can roll up and get through the door without hassle. Where a blind person can read the menu. Where someone with an assistive communication device can place their order and take care of the bill without being made to feel like a nuisance. Where the sound doesn’t ricochet off the walls like the inside of a tin can, so someone who is hard-of-hearing or neurodivergent can carry on a conversation without pain. Where someone with a chronic illness or compromised immune system can feel welcome.

Nearly 30% of adults in the U.S. have a disability, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . The CDC defines disability as “any condition of the body or mind that makes it more difficult for the person with the condition to do certain activities and interact with the world around them.”

The Move To Include Podcast The Move To Include Podcast puts the voices of people with disabilities at the center of the conversation about inclusion... But there’s another way to look at it: the social model of disability, credited to researcher Mike Oliver. The idea is that a significant aspect of limitations is determined by the blueprint of the built world around us, and people’s attitudes toward disability.

“It is society which disables physically impaired people. Disability is something imposed on top of our impairments by the way we are unnecessarily isolated and excluded from full participation in society,” Oliver wrote in the textbook, “ Implementing the Social Model of Disability: Theory and Research .”

If disability is partly determined by design, then what are the barriers? And what are some ways to alleviate that divide?

Not just meeting Americans with Disabilities Act regulations, which many advocates argue is the bare minimum for accessibility standards (not to diminish how monumental the ADA was when signed into law in 1990), but putting forth best practices in universal design and inclusive social dynamics.

local.title: Feds abandon plans for Border Patrol station in downtown Rochester
local.summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is forgoing plans to convert space in the Kenneth B. Keating Federal Building in downtown Rochester into a Border Patrol station, Congressional Democrats say.
local.body:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is forgoing plans to convert space in the Kenneth B. Keating Federal Building in downtown Rochester into a Border Patrol station.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, and House Rep. Joseph Morelle announced the stoppage on Friday, saying the General Services Administration, which oversees the Keating Federal Building, notified the Western District of New York Federal Court that CBP withdrew its request and will explore other options.

“This is a major victory for the people of Rochester who made their voices heard and refused to accept the Trump Administration’s reckless plan to bring immigration detention cells into the heart of our downtown,” Morelle said in a news release. “I’m grateful to Senator Schumer and Senator Gillibrand for their partnership in fighting this proposal, and I will continue fighting to protect our community from Donald Trump’s cruel immigration agenda.”

CBP has expressed interest in moving downtown since 2019 and included the project in its 2025 budget request. Border Patrol planned to convert the space into offices, with at least three temporary holding cells, plus K9 kennels and other features.

The proposal faced major opposition from congressional leaders, residents, and elected officials citing concerns and what they described as inaccurate or incomplete information that the administration released to the public in early May.

WXXI News reached out to CBP for comment on where the agency might look to relocate but had not received a response by publication time.

local.title: Wayne County supervisors appoint new health director
local.summary: The Board of Supervisors approved Jennifer Rodriguez’s appointment at its meeting this week.
local.body:
The Board of Supervisors approved Jennifer Rodriguez’s appointment at its meeting Tuesday morning.

Rodriguez currently is director of Livingston County Health, where she has served since 2013. She succeeds Diane Devlin, who retired in March. Deputy Director Kerry Van Auken has been directing the agency since Devlin’s retirement.

Rodriguez will be paid nearly $166,000. She starts her new position Jan. 4.

She said her decision to take the Wayne position “is rooted in my longstanding passion for public health and my commitment to improving the health and well-being of the communities I serve.”

Rodriguez said she oversaw multiple areas of public health and community services in Livingston County, “which provided me with invaluable leadership experience and a broader understanding of the challenges facing rural communities.” In October, she took on the additional role of interim director of community mental health services in Livingston County following the resignation of Sarah McCumiskey.

She explained that the Wayne County job allows her “to return my full attention to core public health services, preventive health care, and the essential work of improving population health outcomes.”

“At the heart of my decision is something very simple: I believe deeply in the power of prevention, the importance of accessible healthcare, and the ability of local public health departments to make a lasting difference in people’s lives,” Rodriguez continued. “I am grateful for my years in Livingston County and enthusiastic about beginning this next chapter serving the residents of Wayne County. … I am genuinely excited to join Wayne County, learn from its residents and community partners, and work alongside its dedicated public health professionals. I see this transition as an opportunity for both professional growth and a renewed focus on the work that first drew me to public health.”

Rodriguez was named a Women of Excellence honoree by the Rochester Business Journal in 2021. The RBJ said the program celebrates “high-achieving women across the Greater Rochester area for their professional accomplishments, community involvement, and commitment to mentoring.”

local.summary: An area representative is again making a push to have the former NRG plant repowered with natural gas. U.S. Rep. Nick Langworthy this week called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to immediately suspend implementation of New York’s All-Electric Buildings Act and work with the State Legislature to permanently rep
local.body:
An area representative is again making a push to have the former NRG plant repowered with natural gas.

U.S. Rep. Nick Langworthy this week called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to immediately suspend implementation of New York's All-Electric Buildings Act and work with the State Legislature to permanently repeal the law following a new warning from the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) that the state is facing its first-ever projected statewide electricity resource deficiency. Langworthy also renewed his call to repurpose the shuttered Dunkirk coal plant for natural gas.

The Dunkirk location is now owned by Genover, which delivers infrastructure across transmission and distribution, substation, generation, engineering and fleet support -- through its own capabilities and a group of specialized operating companies. It also is being eyed as a potential nuclear site.

"This is a five-alarm warning for Governor Hochul and every legislator in Albany that their dangerous, reckless push to full electrification will have catastrophic consequences if allowed to go forward," said Langworthy. "The findings in this report detail the exact outcome I have been talking about since day one, and why I've fought to block this disastrous law from taking effect. The impact of their policies is no longer theoretical--the facts are at our front door and New Yorkers' safety and security is at grave risk."

According to NYISO's latest Reliability Needs Assessment, New York could face an electricity supply shortfall beginning in 2033, initially estimated at 225 megawatts and growing to more than 1,850 megawatts by 2036. The report underscores the growing strain on an aging electric grid, declining availability of existing power generation, and rising electricity demand.

Langworthy continued, "I am calling on Governor Hochul to permanently halt implementation of her natural gas ban and work with the legislature to officially repeal this misguided mandate. New York needs more reliable and affordable energy, not fewer options. Natural gas is an important part of our energy mix, and families, businesses, and builders should be able to choose the energy sources that make sense for their needs and budgets. Time is of the essence to get more supply into the system and while nuclear is a great part of the equation we can't afford the gaps while we wait for those plants to come online. That's exactly why repurposing the Dunkirk plant to natural gas makes perfect sense."

local.body:
Community Bank plans to close its Central Avenue branch in Dunkirk in the spring, consolidating its banking services at another location nearby.

In a letter dated Nov. 16, the bank informed customers its branch at 345 Central Ave. will close effective Friday, March 19. Banking services offered at that location will be transferred to the branch at 3909 Vineyard Drive in Dunkirk.

The bank said the decision followed a thorough assessment of its branch network and how it can best serve customers as banking needs evolve.

"We understand a branch closing may be inconvenient and we appreciate the trust you have placed in Community Bank," the letter stated. The bank also indicated its team would work to help customers navigate the transition.

Jack Quinn scored twice — once into an empty net — and Zach Benson a
local.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night.

Jack Quinn scored twice -- once into an empty net -- and Zach Benson and Tage Thompson also scored for the Sabres. Buffalo converted on five of its 13 shots in the first two periods. Alex Tuch, Ryan Leonard and Boone Jenner scored Washington, which has fallen to .500 after entering the season with lofty expectations.

Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington’s career lead in assists with his 763rd.

The Capitals have allowed at least five goals in four straight games and six of their last eight. On Wednesday it took them only two periods to do so. Thompson allowed three goals on five shots before being yanked in favor of Charlie Lindgren.

It was the second time in his last six starts Thompson was pulled early.

After Quinn opened the scoring, Dahlin entered the zone on a power play, and when Thompson overplayed him a bit to the near post, the Buffalo defenseman swooped behind the net and wrapped the puck into the vacated other side.

Tuch scored again against his former team. He had two goals against Buffalo, including the winner in overtime, in a game last month.

It was 4-1 after one Thursday, and Tage Thompson scored on the power play near the end of the second. Leonard scored to cap a dominant stretch on the power play for Washington in the third, then Jenner poked the puck in with 10:16 remaining after Buffalo goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen seemed unaware it was loose.

local.title: Other voices: Air traffic system needs reforms
local.summary: And you thought flying in America couldn’t get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to
local.body:
And you thought flying in America couldn't get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to have been routine government failure.

Friday's fiasco, which disrupted millions of travel plans, laid bare the myriad dysfunctions of America's government-run air-traffic control system that have led to repeated system failures and delays. Flyers were left stranded for hours as the FAA tried to diagnose and fix the problem, which officials eventually tied to a new router at a facility in Arkansas.

According to FAA officials, the router along with another one in Texas flooded its communications system with data. It's far from reassuring that one or two malfunctioning devices can take down continental air traffic. Or that the Sherlock Holmeses at the FAA still aren't sure exactly what went wrong.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed either a faulty device or "incompetence" by the contractor L3Harris Technologies that had installed it. HPE, the router manufacturer, said its hardware "did not fail." While Mr. Duffy claimed the government hasn't found evidence of nefarious causes, it's understandable to wonder given that adversaries are stepping up cyberattacks across the U.S. economy and government.

As is their habit, politicians rushed to capitalize on the public misery. Democrats blamed the Administration's new SMART system, which uses AI to analyze airline schedules, weather, airspace conditions, among other things, to prevent flight conflicts that cause delays. There's no evidence the AI system contributed to Friday's problems.

Mr. Duffy on Thursday called for $30 billion in more funding, on top of the $12.5 billion Republicans appropriated in last year's tax bill. After Friday's failure, he raised the demand to $50 billion. But throwing more money at an unaccountable agency will at best be a temporary fix and will reward dysfunction.

In 2003 Congress directed the FAA to modernize America's aging air-traffic system, yet the Government Accountability Office reported in September that the FAA doesn't plan to complete the first phase of upgrades until December 2028. That's a quarter-century.

The GAO also said the FAA lacks a reliable estimate for when the second phase will be done and how much the entire project will cost. This is government incompetence across several administrations at a California bullet-train-to-nowhere level. Criticism from Pete Buttigieg, the Biden transportation secretary, is especially laughable given his obvious failure to improve things over four years in the job. And he apparently wants to run for President again.

entertainment.title: Tom Selleck Had One Issue With Moving His Jesse Stone Movies From CBS To Hallmark
entertainment.summary: Tom Selleck was happy when Hallmark stepped in to continue the popular Jesse Stone TV movie series, but the star had one complaint about the switch.
entertainment.body:
Selleck starred as the title character in eight Jesse Stone films for CBS, with the first one airing in 2005 and the eighth premiering in 2015. An adaptation of Robert B. Parker's novel series, the movies follow a troubled former LAPD detective who gets a job as the police chief of a supposedly quaint Massachusetts town, only to find lots of crime that needs his brand of justice. The movies were a hit; "Jesse Stone: Benefit of the Doubt," the final one CBS aired, drew in nearly 13 million viewers . Despite this, the channel opted against making another

"Bless them, they've done eight of these that always perform far above what's normally in the time slot, but they are constantly perplexed," Selleck told Zap2it . "'We're not in the two-hour-movie business.'"

Hallmark, which had found ratings success rerunning the CBS films, stepped in to make a new movie. "Jesse Stone: Lost in Paradise" premiered in October 2015 . "We have the same production values," Selleck told TV Insider . "I just wish they'd let me say 'son of a b****' a little more. It's hard to make an adult show that has the darkness of Jesse Stone and say, 'Oh, fudge!'"

In 2024, though, the "Magnum, P.I." lead told TV Insider that there was interest in a 10th Jesse Stone film . And, if he had his way, it wouldn't be the last one.

"It looks like now I might have to write [a script for another movie.] It wouldn't be a final one because everybody loves it. Jesse is a great character, and it would be fascinating to find out where he is quite a few years later," Tom Selleck said. entertainment.summary: Cannon was diagnosed with the autoimmune disease in 2012.
entertainment.body:
Nick Cannon revealed Friday (Nov. 20) that he’s been hospitalized amid his battle with lupus, and he’s asking fans to keep him in their prayers.

“#LupusWarrior,” Cannon wrote in his caption, soundtracked by Donny Hathaway’s “A Song for You.” The accompanying photo finds the father of 12 undergoing a series of medical tests while lying in a hospital bed and wearing a PPE mask.

He added in the photo: “This [world emoji] can definitely take a lot out of you. Pray for me y’all!”

Cannon posted a clip to his Instagram Story , as he seemingly prepared to undergo a CT scan. “Have you had a CT before?” a medical professional can be heard asking him off-camera.

Billboard has reached out to a rep for Cannon for further information about his hospitalization.

The Wild ‘n Out creator was diagnosed with the autoimmune disease back in 2012. According to Mayo Clinic , “Lupus is a condition in which the body’s immune system attacks its own tissues and organs. This is called an autoimmune condition. Lupus causes swelling and irritation, called inflammation, that may affect joints, skin, kidneys, blood cells, brain, heart and lungs.”

Among his myriad business commitments, the 46-year-old has been traveling for his Wild ‘n Out Live: The Next Generation tour, which continues Saturday (Nov. 21) at Houston’s Toyota Center. It’s still unknown if he will appear at the show.

entertainment.title: Kylie Cantrall Talks ‘Bold, Grown & Messy’ New Music, How Her Disney Fans ‘Coexist’ With Growing Audience
entertainment.summary: The Disney alum gets candid about her new music era at intimate Moxy Hotels Check-In Sessions.
entertainment.body:
Nestled into a corner of the Moxy Hotel in downtown L.A. this week, Kylie Cantrall sat down with Billboard to chat about her sold-out headlining solo tour, her songwriting process and her new era, post-Disney’s Descendants franchise.

Growing up in the nearby Valley, Cantrall starred in her breakout role as Red in Disney’s Descendants in 2024, and is now the release of her Valley Girl Problems EP on July 24 marks a new chapter for the Venezuelan-American artist.

With her Valley Girl Problems Tour wrapping up last month and anticipation building for her upcoming Jingle Ball LA performance in December, Cantrall surprised fans with an intimate acoustic performance at the Moxy. Reaching out directly to her fanbase through a text message, she offered a more personal, stripped-down evening and a chance to connect in a smaller setting.

Stepping out of her Descendants era, the former Disney star has found a strong connection with listeners through her solo music, which explores themes of teenage heartbreak, friendship breakups and the growing pains of finding yourself. “ Valley Girl Problems was what I was going through at that time. Discovering myself and opening up about the trials and tribulations, and the messier parts,” she says.

Cantrall has described the nine-track project as a reintroduction to herself as an artist, leaning into the very Valley Girl stereotype that has become part of her identity. After landing her Disney breakout role at the age of 17, Los Angeles became an essential part of her journey into the entertainment industry. Rather than shy away from her roots — Valley Girl vocal fry and all — she’s embracing the persona as a reflection of who she is.

That sense of nostalgia also carries into the EP’s sound, with early 2000s pop influences woven throughout the project. It’s no surprise, then, that Cantrall brought in hitmaker Tricky Stewart, best known for co-writing Grammy-winning hits like Rihanna’s “Umbrella” and Beyoncé’s “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It).”

“Tricky made me feel like I had all the answers,” Cantrall says. “He told me to trust my intuition and empowered me to not second guess myself as an artist.”

Despite feeling nervous about entering the writing room and collaborating with such an established name in the industry, Cantrall said Stewart helped bring her ideas to the surface while building her confidence as a songwriter. Reflecting on their time in the studio, she recalled how encouraging Stewart was throughout the creative process, helping her feel more comfortable opening up and finding her voice.

entertainment.title: Mort Weiner, Veteran Label Executive, Dies at 92: ‘His Commitment to Artists and Our Industry Was Superb’
entertainment.summary: Over a career spanning nearly four decades, Weiner held senior positions in sales, promotion, marketing and distribution at several major record labels.
entertainment.body:
Veteran record label executive Mort Weiner died on Oct. 25 at age 92. Over a career spanning nearly four decades, Weiner held senior positions in sales, promotion, marketing and distribution at several major record labels, including Columbia, MGM, Metromedia, Motown, RCA and 20th Century-Fox Records.

Veteran music executive Neil Portnow , former president/CEO of the Recording Academy, tells Billboard , “Mort was a colleague from my first days in L.A. at RCA in the late ‘70’s, and then at 20th Century Fox Records where I hired him to run our marketing, sales and international efforts. I couldn’t have made a better choice because his work, energy and commitment to artists and our industry were superb. But most importantly, I gained a true friendship which has lasted through these many decades. He will be missed by all who had the privilege to work with and know him.”

Weiner began his record company career in 1961 as the Miami branch manager for Dot Records, which had a No. 1 hit on the Billboard Hot 100 that year with Pat Boone ’s “Moody River.” He went on to handle local promotion for Columbia Records in Miami, where he helped build early interest in Simon & Garfunkel. In 1966, he took responsibility for promotion across 11 Southern states for Columbia’s Date label. He joined MGM and was named national singles sales manager for Verve and Verve/Forecast in 1967. Weiner joined Metromedia Records around the time of its launch in late 1968 and rose from Eastern regional promotion to director of national sales and then to national director of marketing and merchandising. The label’s biggest star was Bobby Sherman , one of the top teen pop stars of the era. Sherman landed four top 10 Hot 100 hits for Metromedia from 1969-70, including “Easy Come, Easy Go” and “Julie, Do Ya Love Me.” Weiner joined Motown Records in its Los Angeles office, where he served as executive administrator of promotion. His tenure included the label’s Anthology franchise, which drew on Motown’s priceless catalog. The Anthology series began in 1973 with a Temptations collection that rode the Billboard 200 for six months and went platinum. While at Motown, Weiner was named a finalist for record company executive of the year at Bobby Poe ’s Radio/Record Seminar and Awards Banquet. In 1975, Weiner moved to RCA as the sales and promotion manager for custom labels. He went on to direct custom label sales and, in 1977, became director of pop product merchandising, overseeing RCA’s pop product managers. His work with affiliated labels included Silver Convention’s “Fly, Robin, Fly” on Midland International (a Hot 100-topping, Grammy-winning smash from 1975), the soundtrack to The Omen on Tattoo Records, and releases by The Whispers and Carrie Lucas on Soul Train Records. Jefferson Starship thanked him in the credits to its 1978 album Earth , which made the top five on the Billboard 200 and went platinum. In 1979, Weiner joined 20th Century-Fox Records as director of sales and merchandising. He became vp of sales and merchandising in 1980. That same year, label president Portnow put him in charge of international operations. As part of the label’s push to expand sales abroad, Weiner met with executives at RCA, which handled the label’s international distribution. In an October 1980 Billboard interview, Portnow pointed to singer-songwriter Jim Photoglo ’s success in Japan as an example of the label’s increased presence overseas. Weiner later served as vp of sales and distribution at Total Experience Records, where he helped introduce a program that used lower suggested retail prices and dealer incentives to support new artists. He returned to Motown in 1987 as vp of sales and distribution, a newly created position at the time. Smokey Robinson had back-to-back top 10 hits on the Hot 100 that year: “Just to See Her” (which won a Grammy) and “One Heartbeat.” Weiner’s later work took him into record and compact disc manufacturing, including a role as vp of sales at Nimbus Manufacturing. From his early days promoting singles in Miami to his work in national distribution and CD manufacturing, Weiner spent his career on the business side of getting music heard.

entertainment.title: Jennifer Lopez savagely throws movie studios under the bus for film flopping at box office
entertainment.summary: "Kiss of the Spider Woman" cost $30 million to produce and earned less than $1.8 million at the worldwide box office.
entertainment.body:
Jennifer Lopez blamed an alleged lack of a sufficient marketing budget for her 2025 adaptation of “Kiss of the Spider Woman” bombing at the box office.

During Thursday’s episode of The New York Times’ “Popcast” podcast , Lopez, who starred in the musical drama alongside Tonatiuh and Diego Luna, reflected on the film’s disappointing performance while answering a question about a time things hadn’t gone her way in her career.

“I would have liked to have had a bigger marketing budget for ‘Kiss of the Spider Woman,'” she said while promoting her upcoming concert special, “The JLO Show.”

“I think it was underseen, and I also had higher hopes for it when I first started the project. It was such a great role for me,” she added.

Lopez, 57, went on to acknowledge that while the film’s marketing may have contributed to its poor performance, she also felt its execution fell short of expectations.

“Kiss of the Spider Woman,” which was based on John Kander and Fred Ebb’s 1993 Tony Award-winning Broadway musical of the same name, cost Lionsgate, Roadside Attractions and LD Entertainment $30 million to produce . Page Six has reached out to the studios for comment.

At the time of its release, the film — which was written and directed by Bill Condon — was expected to earn a modest $2 million at the box office during its opening weekend. Ultimately, it grossed less than $1.8 million worldwide.

Elsewhere during the podcast, Lopez addressed what she believes are misconceptions about her career as an actress.

entertainment.title: 5 Best Historical Drama Series Of The '80s, Ranked
entertainment.summary: Often grand in scope and with stories so big that they're made for the multi-episode format, these are some of the best historical drama series of the '80s.
entertainment.body:
Whether telling the story of a well-known historical figure or spinning a yarn about a fictional character in the midst of an actual era, the best historical dramas of the '80s all stand the test of time themselves. It is hard to narrow it down to five, so there are a couple of notable omissions. "Lonesome Dove" and "The Thorn Birds" are two of the most acclaimed miniseries of the '80s and both are dramas that take place in the past. However, the former is an exceptional Western and the latter is a sweeping saga about a fictional family. They're each distinct subgenres of their own and not necessarily what immediately comes to mind when one thinks "historical drama."

Having set those two classic series aside, let's take a look at five of the best historical dramas of the '80s.

CBS Unlike in a certain hit Broadway musical , nobody raps in this story of a Founding Father's life. The 1984 miniseries "George Washington," which aired on CBS in April 1983, was a success all the same. Based on a biography of the first president by James Thomas Flexner, "George Washington" begins with Washington's upbringing as a young man in the French and Indian War and follows him through the Revolutionary War. A sequel series in 1986, "George Washington II: The Forging of a Nation" tackled his presidency, but it was not as big of a success as the first show.

Barry Bostwick, best known for "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" and "Spin City," plays the title character, and a glowing New York Times review praised his emotional performance. The Times also endorsed the ambitious series as a whole, noting that its comprehensive telling of Washington's story helped paint a fuller picture of the man on the dollar bill than audiences were perhaps used to at the time. Variety's review noted that the show made familiar U.S. history fresh and entertaining. Viewed now, "George Washington" doesn't exactly reinvent the historical bioseries, but it's an extremely competent and rewarding example of the form. Our first president deserves a first-rate bioseries, don't you think?

"George Washington" was nominated for six Emmy Awards, though it ultimately went home empty handed.

Based on "The Antagonists," a 1971 novel by Ernest K. Gann which told a heavily fictionalized account of the historical event due to a lack of extensive firsthand records of what actually happened, "Masada" was originally intended to be a movie but the scope of the story was simply too big for one feature film. ABC thought it had potential as a miniseries, and spent $25 million on the resulting 8-hour show. The budget shows on the screen; filmed on-location in Israel, "Masada" is a worthy swords and sandals epic, boasting a great, sympathetic villain performance from O'Toole. It all builds to the tragic end; after finally breaking through in the monthslong siege, Silva finds that everybody in the fortress has committed suicide rather than submit to Rome.

entertainment.title: Tristan Thompson Reveals His “Home Run” Investment in Anthropic AI
